edges: Dolin describes spermaceti candles as the foundation of the colonial whale trade that grew into the golden age.
The collapse of Dutch whaling left the northern and Atlantic fishery to the Americans, as the folio reads Ellis and Dolin together.
Schivelbusch presents gaslight as the next step beyond the oil lamp that Argand had perfected.
Sperm and whale oils fed the lamps of the period, of which the Argand burner was the best.
Ward lists Chevreul’s chemistry among the three developments that made soap manufacture industrial.
Steam, Leblanc soda and Chevreul together make soap an industrial product, as Ward says.
Chevreul’s chemistry is one of the three components of industrial soap in Ward’s account.
Ward reads the doubling of consumption as the result of the industrial capacity to make soap cheaply.
The excise duty gives the record from which Ward counts consumption.
Industrial chemistry lets makers use a wider range of oils than the olive.
Law argues that the end of the slave trade turned the Biafran ports to palm oil, whose British imports rose tenfold.
The tonnages shipped from Old Calabar and Bonny make up the British imports of Law’s table.
Liverpool’s former slavers are among the importers of this oil.
Lynn and Hopkins explain the tenfold rise in British palm-oil imports by industrial demand for lubricants, soap and candles.
Bristol’s role as a soap-making centre is the soap side of the palm-oil demand.
Law argues that after 1807 the oil trade increased slavery within West Africa.
Imported oils entering the soap kettles of Marseille and Bristol belong to the same industrial demand for oils.
Tasmania’s bay whalers and Nantucket’s deep-sea fleet worked the same decades with different methods.
New Zealand’s shore stations copied the bay-whaling methods that the Derwent crews had developed.
Yankee ships at Walvis Bay are the south-east Atlantic end of the Nantucket and New Bedford fishery.
Honolulu and Lahaina were the Pacific stopping-off points for the Nantucket and New Bedford fleet at its peak.
The coconut estates of Penang and the palm-oil boom on the Bight of Biafra are two tropical oil frontiers of the same decades.
